items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to determine trigonometric ratios of large angles in degrees.

Content:
For example, suppose we wish to calculate the value of

Content:
[MATH: \sin\left(7,230^\circ\right).]

Content:
Trigonometric ratios like sine and cosine repeat every [MATH: 360^\circ] (full turns). So, instead of evaluating a large angle directly, we reduce it to a smaller, coterminal angle between [MATH: 0^\circ] and
[MATH: 360^\circ.]

Content:
To do this, we first find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: 7,230^\circ] and lies in the range [MATH: [0,360^\circ).]

Content:
Recall that coterminal angles differ by a multiple of [MATH: 360^\circ.] So, we divide [MATH: 7,230] by [MATH: 360] with remainder:

Content:
[MATH: 7,230 \div 360 = 20 \ \text{R} \ 30]

Content:
Therefore, we can express [MATH: 7,230] as a multiple if [MATH: 360] plus our remainder as follows:
[MATH: 7,230 = 20 \cdot 360 + 30.]

Content:
Adding in our degree symbol, we have

Content:
[MATH: 7, 230^{∘} = 20 ⋅ 360^{∘} + 30^{∘}.]

Content:
So, we can reduce our large angle of [MATH: 7,230^\circ] by [MATH: 20] full turns of [MATH: 360^\circ,] since adding or subtracting a full turn doesn't change the sine:

Content:
[MATH: \sin\left(7,230^\circ\right) = \sin\left({\color{blue}20 \cdot 360^\circ} + 30^\circ\right) = \sin\left(30^\circ\right).]

Content:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/33622094d22c5e6d891e89ba031f2da9]

Content:
From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 30^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right).]

Content:
Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin\left(30^\circ\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: \sin\left(7,230^\circ\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: 8,235^\circ] and lies in the range [MATH: [0,360^\circ).]

Recall that coterminal angles differ by a multiple of [MATH: 360^\circ.] So, we divide [MATH: 8,235] by [MATH: 360] with remainder:

[MATH: 8,235 \div 360 = 22\ \text{R} \ 315]

Therefore, [MATH: 8,235= 22\cdot 360 + 315.]

As a result, we have

[MATH: 8, 235^{∘} = 22 ⋅ 360^{∘} + 315^{∘}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \sin \left(8,235^\circ\right) = \sin \left(315^\circ\right).]

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 315^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right).]

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin\left(315^\circ\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \sin\left(8,235^\circ\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the value of [MATH: \tan\left(7,140^\circ\right).]
sections.readable_text: Find the value of [MATH: \tan\left(7,140^\circ\right).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: 7,140^\circ] and lies in the range [MATH: [0^\circ,360^\circ).]

Recall that coterminal angles differ by a multiple of [MATH: 360^\circ.]

So, we divide [MATH: 7,140] by [MATH: 360] with remainder:

[MATH: 7,140 \div 360 = 19 \ \text{R} \ 300]

As a result, we have

[MATH: 7,140^\circ = 19 \cdot 360^\circ + 300^\circ.]

Therefore, [MATH: \tan(7,140^\circ) = \tan(300^\circ).]

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 300^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right).]

  • Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: x]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \cos \left(300^\circ \right) = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

  • Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin \left(300^\circ \right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.]

Therefore, using the fact that [MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},] we have

[MATH: \tan(300^\circ) = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = -\sqrt{3}.]

Finally, [MATH: \tan(7,140^\circ) = -\sqrt{3}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \tan(7,140^\circ) = \tan(300^\circ).]

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

[IMG: /graphics/b62a3d30265eff8bd749e7e55163c507]

From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 300^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right).]

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: x]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \cos \left(300^\circ \right) = \dfrac{1}{2}.]
- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin \left(300^\circ \right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.]

Therefore, using the fact that [MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},] we have
